title: Enhanced Sensitivity near a Quantum Exceptional Point in the Absence of Engineered Dissipation
authors: Réouven Assouly, Harry Hanlim Kang, Aziza Almanakly, Michael A. Gingras, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Hannah Stickler, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Max Hays, Jeffrey A. Grover, William D. Oliver
abstract: Non-Hermitian systems exhibit phenomena absent from Hermitian systems, including exceptional points (EPs), at which two or more eigenvectors coalesce. Conventional implementations rely on gain and loss, which strongly limit quantum coherence. Here, following a proposal by Wang and Clerk (PRA 2019), we realize a closed four-mode quantum system that emulates the dynamics of a PT dimer - two coupled resonators with balanced gain and loss - without engineered dissipation. The four modes are implemented as harmonics of a superconducting coplanar-waveguide resonator, with parametric couplings engineered using a current-pumped SNAIL. We use this device as a sensor for small variations in the PT dimer coupling strength. From signal-to-noise-ratio measurements, we observe enhanced sensitivity near the EP in a non-quantum-limited regime.
summary: The authors realized a four-mode superconducting circuit to simulate the dynamics of a PT dimer without using engineered loss or gain. They successfully demonstrated enhanced sensitivity near the Quantum Exceptional Point by monitoring supermode evolution, confirming that such non-Hermitian phenomena can be robustly studied in coherent quantum systems.
main_problem: The goal was to demonstrate enhanced quantum sensing near a Quantum Exceptional Point (EP) in a non-Hermitian system without relying on engineered gain and loss mechanisms.
main_result: The experiment successfully emulated PT dimer dynamics using coherent parametric drives, achieving enhanced sensitivity near the EP in a regime limited by classical noise rather than quantum backaction.
method: The researchers used a superconducting coplanar-waveguide resonator coupled to a SNAIL to realize and probe the four-mode system Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The physical system is a closed four-mode bosonic circuit emulating a PT dimer, whose dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian involving parametric couplings ($\hat{H} \propto g (\hat{a}^\dagger_1\hat{a}_2 - \hat{a}^\dagger_3\hat{a}_4) + i\gamma/2 (\hat{a}^\dagger_1\hat{a}^\dagger_4 - \hat{a}^\dagger_2\hat{a}^\dagger_3) + H.c.$).
key_observables: Supermode amplitudes ($\alpha_1, \alpha_2$), eigenvalue splitting ($|\omega_+ - \omega_-|$), and the sensitivity metric $\eta_i(	ilde{g}, t)$.
important_parameters: The EP occurs at $g = \gamma/2$; the system is characterized by coupling strengths $g$ and decay rates $\gamma$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed enhanced sensitivity near the EP is dominated by the derivative of the supermode amplitude with respect to the coupling strength, rather than noise reduction.
figures_summary: Figures show mode frequency vs. flux bias (Fig. 2a), time evolution of supermodes ($\alpha_1, \alpha_2$) showing Rabi-like oscillations near the EP (Fig. 4), and sensitivity plots ($\eta_i$ maximized at the EP) (Fig. 5).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the theoretical framework of PT dimers and EPs. It then details the experimental realization using superconducting circuits, followed by calibration procedures for individual modes and parametric drives. Finally, it presents time-domain measurements demonstrating the controlled dynamics and enhanced sensing near the EP.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial experimental demonstration of non-Hermitian physics (EPs) in a solid-state platform, moving beyond simple gain/loss implementations to use purely coherent parametric drives for quantum simulation and sensing.

At zero flux, the resonant frequency shifts down- ward with increasing power, indicating a negative Kerr coef- ficient.
